claim: Circadian clocks are genetically encoded, self-sustained molecular oscillators that drive biological rhythms with a period close to 24 hr.
source: Circadian clocks are genetically encoded, self-sustained molecular oscillators that drive biological rhythms with a period close to 24 hr (Partch et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Partch et al., 2014

claim: Circadian clocks are found in most organisms and even in cultured tissues and cells.
source: They are found in most organisms and even in cultured tissues and cells (Balsalobre et al., 1998; Brown et al., 2012; Yoo et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Balsalobre et al., 1998; Brown et al., 2012; Yoo et al., 2004

claim: In mammals, circadian clocks are organized in a network controlled by a master pacemaker in the hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN).
source: In mammals, these clocks are organized in a network controlled by a master pacemaker in the hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) (Dibner et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dibner et al., 2010

claim: Physiological processes such as energy metabolism, locomotion, hormone secretion, and cognitive functions are subject to circadian regulation.
source: Physiological processes such as energy metabolism, locomotion, hormone secretion, and cognitive functions are subject to circadian regulation (Bass and Takahashi, 2010; Gerstner and Yin, 2010; Panda, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bass and Takahashi, 2010; Gerstner and Yin, 2010; Panda, 2016

claim: In each tissue approximately 10% of the transcriptome is under the control of the circadian clock.
source: The influence of circadian rhythmicity is highlighted by the fact that in each tissue ~10% of the transcriptome is under the control of the circadian clock (Zhang et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2014

claim: Disruption of circadian rhythms is tied to the development of various diseases including metabolic disorders and cancer.
source: that disruption of circadian rhythms is tied to the development of various diseases including metabolic disorders and cancer (Bedrosian et al., 2016; Musiek and Holtzman, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bedrosian et al., 2016; Musiek and Holtzman, 2016

claim: The molecular circadian oscillator consists of interlinked positive and negative feedback elements.
source: The molecular circadian oscillator consists of interlinked positive and negative feedback elements (Reppert and Weaver, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reppert and Weaver, 2002

claim: CLOCK and BMAL1 form heterodimers that bind to E-box promoter elements.
source: Positive components are the heterodimers of CLOCK (circadian locomotor output cycles kaput) and BMAL1 (brain and muscle ARNT-like protein 1) that bind to E-box promoter elements of Per1-3 (Period), Cry1/2 (Cryptochome) and Rev-ErbAα/β (Nr1d1/2; nuclear receptor subfamily 1, group D, members 1 and 2) that encode repressor proteins PER, CRY and NR1D (Takahashi, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Takahashi, 2017

claim: Genome-wide analysis revealed temporally restricted chromatin associations of circadian activators and repressors in the course of the circadian day.
source: Genome-wide analysis of core circadian regulators revealed temporally restricted chromatin associations of circadian activators and repressors in the course of the circadian day (Koike et al., 2012; Menet et al., 2012; Rey et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Koike et al., 2012; Menet et al., 2012; Rey et al., 2011

claim: At the onset of the circadian cycle, repressor CRY1 is part of the chromatin-bound CLOCK-BMAL1 complex located near transcriptionally silent RNA polymerase II.
source: It is proposed that at the onset of the circadian cycle repressor CRY1 is part of the chromatin-bound CLOCK-BMAL1-complex located near transcriptionally silent RNA polymerase II (Pol II).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koike et al., 2012 in the following sentence

claim: Upon degradation of CRY1, coactivators such as CBP/p300 are recruited followed by Per and Cry transcription.
source: Upon degradation of CRY1, coactivators such as CBP/p300 are recruited followed by Per and Cry transcription.
evidence: Supported by citation to Koike et al., 2012 in the following sentence

claim: During the repression phase, newly synthesized CRY2 and PER proteins associate with CLOCK-BMAL1, thereby shutting down their own transcription.
source: During the repression phase of the circadian cycle, newly synthesized CRY2 and PER proteins associate with CLOCK-BMAL1, thereby shutting down their own transcription (Koike et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koike et al., 2012

claim: Recruitment of CRY to the CLOCK-BMAL1 heterodimer is facilitated by acetylation of BMAL1 at lysine 538 by the acetyltransferase activity attributed to CLOCK.
source: Recruitment of CRY to the CLOCK-BMAL1 heterodimer is facilitated by acetylation of BMAL1 at lysine 538 by the acetyltransferase activity attributed to CLOCK (Doi et al., 2006; Hirayama et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Doi et al., 2006; Hirayama et al., 2007

claim: BMAL1 acetylation peaks during the repression phase.
source: BMAL1 acetylation peaks during the repression phase (Hirayama et al., 2007), although data by Nakakata and co-workers (Nakahata et al., 2008; Nakahata et al., 2009) suggest that the presence of acetylated BMAL1 extends into the activation phase.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hirayama et al., 2007

claim: The presence of acetylated BMAL1 extends into the activation phase.
source: BMAL1 acetylation peaks during the repression phase (Hirayama et al., 2007), although data by Nakakata and co-workers (Nakahata et al., 2008; Nakahata et al., 2009) suggest that the presence of acetylated BMAL1 extends into the activation phase.
evidence: Supported by citations to Nakahata et al., 2008; Nakahata et al., 2009

claim: Rate-limiting steps that regulate transcription include the recruitment of Pol II to promoters and Pol II release from promoter-proximal pause sites.
source: Well-recognized, rate-limiting steps that regulate transcription are the recruitment of Pol II to promoters and Pol II release from promoter-proximal pause sites (Jonkers and Lis, 2015; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jonkers and Lis, 2015; Liu et al., 2015

claim: Pause release of Pol II and the transition to productive elongation requires the activity of the P-TEFb complex, composed of T-type cyclins and CDK9.
source: Pause release of Pol II and the transition to productive elongation requires the activity of the P-TEFb (positive transcription elongation factor b) complex, composed of T-type cyclins and CDK9 (cyclin-dependent kinase 9) (Jonkers and Lis, 2015; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jonkers and Lis, 2015; Liu et al., 2015

claim: P-TEFb is recruited to promoters through interaction with specific transcription factors and other proteins like BRD4 and SEC.
source: P-TEFb is recruited to promoters through interaction with specific transcription factors and other proteins like BRD4 (bromodomain-containing protein 4) and SEC (super elongation complex) (Jonkers and Lis, 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Luo et al., 2012; Shi and Vakoc, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jonkers and Lis, 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Luo et al., 2012; Shi and Vakoc, 2014

claim: After recruitment, P-TEFb phosphorylates the carboxy-terminal domain (CTD) of Pol II at Ser2 and additionally phosphorylates the pausing factors NELF and DSIF.
source: After such recruitment, P-TEFb phosphorylates the carboxy-terminal domain (CTD) of Pol II at Ser2 and additionally phosphorylates the pausing factors NELF (negative elongation factor) and DSIF (DRB sensitivity inducing factor).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of P-TEFb function

claim: Upon phosphorylation, NELF is evicted from Pol II and DSIF becomes a positive elongation factor.
source: Upon phosphorylation, NELF is evicted from Pol II and DSIF becomes a positive elongation factor.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of transcription elongation

claim: Pol II pausing serves as a checkpoint allowing for rapid and synchronous expression of genes.
source: Pol II pausing serves as a checkpoint allowing for rapid and synchronous expression of genes (Boettiger and Levine, 2009; Gilchrist et al., 2012; Lagha et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boettiger and Levine, 2009; Gilchrist et al., 2012; Lagha et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2015

claim: BRD4 is a member of the bromo-domain and extra terminal domain (BET) protein family which bind through their bromo-domains to acetylated lysines of histones and of transcription factors.
source: BRD4 is a member of the bromo-domain and extra terminal domain (BET) protein family which bind through their bromo-domains to acetylated lysines of histones and of transcription factors (Shi and Vakoc, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shi and Vakoc, 2014

claim: Bound BRD4 recruits P-TEFb to promoter proximal paused Pol II.
source: Bound BRD4 recruits P-TEFb to promoter proximal paused Pol II (Jonkers and Lis, 2015; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jonkers and Lis, 2015; Liu et al., 2015

claim: Small molecule inhibitors that block BRD4 (e.g. JQ1) from binding to acetylated lysines prevent productive elongation.
source: Small molecule inhibitors that block BRD4 (e.g. JQ1) from binding to acetylated lysines prevent productive elongation (Shi and Vakoc, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shi and Vakoc, 2014

claim: BRD4 protein is a key player in the regulation of productive transcription elongation.
source: Thus BRD4 protein is a key player in the regulation of productive transcription elongation.
evidence: Inferred from the preceding statements about BRD4 function

claim: Acetyltransferases that acetylate BRD4 binding partners would play an important role in regulating Pol II pause release.
source: Therefore, acetyltransferases that acetylate BRD4 binding partners would play an important role in regulating Pol II pause release.
evidence: Inferred from the role of BRD4 in recruiting P-TEFb

claim: The lysine acetyltransferase TIP60 is recruited to active promoters.
source: The lysine acetyltransferase TIP60 (60 kDa Tat-interactive protein) is recruited to active promoters (Ravens et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ravens et al., 2015

claim: TIP60 plays a role in early steps of transcription elongation in mammals and flies.
source: and plays a role in early steps of transcription elongation in mammals and flies (Kusch et al., 2014; Ravens et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kusch et al., 2014; Ravens et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2014

claim: TIP60 is an essential protein.
source: TIP60 is an essential protein (Hu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2009

claim: During the activation phase of the circadian cycle, TIP60 acetylates BMAL1, which triggers recruitment of the BRD4-P-TEFb complex to E-box-containing circadian promoters leading to Pol II pause release and productive elongation of circadian transcripts.
source: Here we provide evidence that TIP60 is a critical component of the circadian clock. During the activation phase of the circadian cycle, TIP60 acetylates BMAL1, which triggers recruitment of the BRD4-P-TEFb complex to E-box-containing circadian promoters leading to Pol II pause release and productive elongation of circadian transcripts.
evidence: This is the main claim of the study, supported by multiple experiments described in the Results section

claim: The control of BRD4-P-TEFb recruitment is a novel temporal checkpoint in the circadian clock cycle.
source: We propose that the control of BRD4-P-TEFb recruitment is a novel temporal checkpoint in the circadian clock cycle.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings

claim: Treatment of Bmal1-LUC fibroblasts with flavopiridol suppressed the amplitude of luciferase activity rhythms in a dose dependent manner concomitant with an increased period length.
source: In the presence of flavopiridol (FP), a potent inhibitor of the CDK9 subunit of P-TEFb (Rahl et al., 2010), the amplitude of luciferase activity rhythms was suppressed in a dose dependent manner concomitant with an increased period length until, at high doses, the rhythm was fully lost (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Treatment of fibroblasts with flavopiridol strongly reduced endogenous mRNA expression levels of Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1.
source: Treatment of fibroblasts with FP also strongly reduced endogenous mRNA expression levels of Dbp (D-site albumin promoter binding protein), Per1, and Nr1d1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) that are direct CLOCK-BMAL1 targets (Stratmann et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1 are direct CLOCK-BMAL1 targets.
source: Treatment of fibroblasts with FP also strongly reduced endogenous mRNA expression levels of Dbp (D-site albumin promoter binding protein), Per1, and Nr1d1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) that are direct CLOCK-BMAL1 targets (Stratmann et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stratmann et al., 2012

claim: Circadian clock gene regulation occurs at the level of Pol II pause release and productive elongation.
source: These findings suggest that circadian clock gene regulation not only occurs at the initiation of transcription (Le Martelot et al., 2012) but also at the level of Pol II pause release and productive elongation.
evidence: Inferred from the flavopiridol experiments showing effects on circadian rhythms

claim: JQ1 treatment of Bmal1-LUC reporter fibroblasts dampened luciferase activity rhythms in a dose-dependent manner and evoked a lengthening of the period.
source: JQ1 treatment of Bmal1-LUC reporter fibroblasts dampened luciferase activity rhythms in a dose-dependent manner and evoked a lengthening of the period (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: JQ1 resulted in a strong dampening of the rhythm of endogenous Dbp expression.
source: JQ1 also resulted in a strong dampening of the rhythm of endogenous Dbp expression in these cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: In the presence of JQ1, enrichment of BRD4 and CDK9 at the transcription start site (TSS) of Dbp was markedly reduced.
source: In the presence of JQ1, enrichment of BRD4 and CDK9 at the transcription start site (TSS) of Dbp was markedly reduced (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Ser2 phosphorylation of Pol II at the 3'-end of Dbp was strongly diminished by JQ1 treatment.
source: Ser2 phosphorylation of Pol II, at the 3'-end of Dbp, was strongly diminished (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) suggesting that Pol II pause release had been suppressed (Harlen and Churchman, 2017).
evidence: Supported by ChIP experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: Reduced Ser2 phosphorylation of Pol II suggests that Pol II pause release had been suppressed.
source: Ser2 phosphorylation of Pol II, at the 3'-end of Dbp, was strongly diminished (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) suggesting that Pol II pause release had been suppressed (Harlen and Churchman, 2017).
evidence: Inferred from the reduction in Ser2 phosphorylation, supported by citation to Harlen and Churchman, 2017

claim: BRD4 inhibition by JQ1 strongly reduced endogenous expression levels of Dbp mRNA but had no effect on mRNA or protein levels of ectopically expressed Bmal1-myc.
source: BRD4 inhibition by JQ1 strongly reduced endogenous expression levels of Dbp mRNA but had no effect on mRNA or protein levels of Bmal1-myc (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E

claim: BRD4 inhibition did not affect endogenous mRNA or protein levels of Bmal1 in Bmal1-LUC fibroblasts at 24 hr after Dex synchronization.
source: Furthermore, BRD4 inhibition neither affected endogenous mRNA nor protein levels of Bmal1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) in Bmal1-LUC fibroblasts at 24 hr after Dex synchronization.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F

claim: The binding of BMAL1 and of acetylated BMAL1 to the Dbp promoter was not affected by BRD4 inhibition.
source: Finally, the binding of BMAL1 and of acetylated BMAL1 (AcBMAL1) to the Dbp promoter was not affected by BRD4 inhibition in these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by ChIP experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G

claim: For the circadian clock-controlled gene Dbp, Pol II pause release may serve as an important regulatory step of its transcription.
source: Together, our JQ1 inhibitor studies suggest that BRD4-P-TEFb is recruited to the E-box-containing clock-controlled gene Dbp which subsequently allows Pol II pause release and transcription elongation. Thus, for this circadian clock-controlled gene, Pol II pause release may serve as an important regulatory step of its transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the JQ1 inhibitor experiments

claim: In CLOCK-deficient fibroblasts, BMAL1 was acetylated at Lys538 to a similar extent as observed in wildtype cells.
source: However, we found that in CLOCK-deficient fibroblasts BMAL1 was acetylated at Lys538 to a similar extent as observed in wildtype cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Both CLOCK and CLOCKmutA showed a minimal increase of BMAL1 acetylation compared to a control.
source: We found that both CLOCK variants showed a minimal increase of BMAL1 acetylation compared to a control (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: BMAL1 acetylation levels in the presence of CLOCK or CLOCKmutA were indistinguishable.
source: Importantly, BMAL1 acetylation levels in the presence of CLOCK or CLOCKmutA were indistinguishable.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data in Figure 3B

claim: There exist alternative acetyltransferases that catalyze BMAL1 acetylation.
source: Together, these data suggest the existence of alternative acetyltransferases that catalyze BMAL1 acetylation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that BMAL1 is acetylated in CLOCK-deficient cells

claim: TIP60 co-purifies with CLOCK-BMAL1.
source: A candidate is TIP60 that co-purifies with CLOCK-BMAL1 (Doi et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Doi et al., 2006

claim: TIP60 acetylates a broad range of transcription factors.
source: A candidate is TIP60 that co-purifies with CLOCK-BMAL1 (Doi et al., 2006) and acetylates a broad range of transcription factors (Judes et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Judes et al., 2015

claim: Addition of TIP60, but not enzymatically inactive TIP60C369A;E403Q, strongly enhanced BMAL1 acetylation.
source: Addition of TIP60, but not enzymatically inactive TIP60C369A;E403Q (Yang et al., 2012), strongly enhanced BMAL1 acetylation (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: All offspring carrying two copies of the knock-in Cre allele (Syt10Cre/Cre Tip60fl/-) and half of the mice carrying one copy of the knock-in Cre allele (Syt10Cre/+Tip60 fl/-) became immediately arrhythmic upon release into constant darkness.
source: All offspring carrying two copies of the knock-in Cre allele (Syt10Cre/Cre Tip60fl/-) and half of the mice carrying one copy of the knock-in Cre allele (Syt10Cre/+Tip60 fl/-) became immediately arrhythmic upon release into constant darkness (DD) (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: The rest of the Syt10Cre/+Tip60 fl/- mice showed either longer (29%) or normal (21%) free-running periods.
source: The rest of the Syt10Cre/+Tip60 fl/- mice showed either longer (29%) or normal (21%) free-running periods.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data analysis

claim: Immunohistochemical staining for TIP60 in the SCN showed nuclear signal, which was absent in arrhythmic Syt10Cre/+Tip60 fl/- mice.
source: Immunohistochemical staining for TIP60 in the SCN showed nuclear signal, which was absent in arrhythmic Syt10Cre/+Tip60 fl/- mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Circadian expression patterns of Per1, Dbp, and Bmal1 in the SCN were severely dampened in arrhythmic Syt10Cre/+Tip60 fl/- mice.
source: Moreover, circadian expression patterns of Per1, Dbp, and Bmal1 in the SCN were severely dampened (Figure 4D) in line with the behavioral arrhythmicity observed in these animals.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Nuclear staining of SCN sections showed no obvious changes in SCN morphology or in the number of SCN cells in TIP60-deficient animals.
source: Nuclear staining of SCN sections from Syt10Cre/+Tip60+/+ and arrhythmic Syt10Cre/+Tip60 fl/- mice showed no obvious changes in SCN morphology or in the number of SCN cells (control: 827 ± 60 cells per section; mutant: 850 ± 68 cells per section).
evidence: Supported by cell counting data

claim: No TUNEL signal, indicating apoptotic cells, could be detected in the SCN of TIP60-deficient animals.
source: In addition, no TUNEL signal, indicating apoptotic cells, could be detected in the SCN of TIP60-deficient animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: SCN cells were fully viable after deletion of Tip60.
source: Together, these experiments indicate that SCN cells were fully viable after deletion of Tip60.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of apoptosis and normal cell numbers

claim: Deletion of TIP60 in confluent MEFs resulted in a major dampening of the rhythmic expression of the luciferase reporter and a significantly reduced expression of endogenous clock genes.
source: Deletion resulted in a major dampening of the rhythmic expression of the luciferase reporter and a significantly reduced expression of endogenous clock genes (Figure 4E and F), but not of several housekeeping genes (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence and mRNA expression data shown in Figure 4E and F

claim: The deletion of TIP60 in confluent MEFs did not affect cell viability.
source: The deletion of TIP60 in confluent MEFs did not affect cell viability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: Adenoviral transduction itself did not alter the circadian rhythm of a luciferase reporter.
source: nor did adenoviral transduction itself alter the circadian rhythm of a luciferase reporter (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F

claim: Abrogation of TIP60 function has major effects on locomotor activity and the rhythmic expression of clock genes in the SCN in vivo and in postmitotic MEFs.
source: Thus, abrogation of TIP60 function has major effects on locomotor activity and the rhythmic expression of clock genes in the SCN in vivo and in postmitotic MEFs.
evidence: Inferred from the combined in vivo and in vitro experimental results

claim: Lys538 of BMAL1 was acetylated by TIP60 in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Co-transfection experiments showed that Lys538 of BMAL1 was acetylated by TIP60 in a dose-dependent manner and that acetyltransferase-deficient TIP60C369A;E403Q (Yang et al., 2012) led to baseline acetylation levels of BMAL1 similar to mock transfected cells (Figure 3B; Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by co-transfection experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 5A

claim: Acetyltransferase-deficient TIP60C369A;E403Q led to baseline acetylation levels of BMAL1 similar to mock transfected cells.
source: Co-transfection experiments showed that Lys538 of BMAL1 was acetylated by TIP60 in a dose-dependent manner and that acetyltransferase-deficient TIP60C369A;E403Q (Yang et al., 2012) led to baseline acetylation levels of BMAL1 similar to mock transfected cells (Figure 3B; Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by co-transfection experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 5A

claim: Lys538 appeared to be the predominant lysine acetylated by TIP60 as the signal obtained with an anti-pan-AcK antibody was strongly diminished in cells co-transfected with BMAL1K538R and TIP60.
source: Lys538 appeared to be the predominant lysine acetylated by TIP60 as the signal obtained with an anti-pan-AcK antibody was strongly diminished in cells co-transfected with BMAL1K538R and TIP60 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: TIP60 co-precipitated with wildtype and BMAL1K538R suggesting an interaction between the two proteins.
source: TIP60 co-precipitated with wildtype and BMAL1K538R suggesting an interaction between the two proteins (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: Acetylation of BMAL1 did not influence the interaction between BMAL1 and TIP60.
source: Acetylation of BMAL1 did not influence this interaction.
evidence: Inferred from the co-precipitation of TIP60 with both wildtype and BMAL1K538R

claim: Both BMAL1 and TIP60V5 proteins bound to the E-boxes of the Dbp gene.
source: Both, BMAL1 and TIP60V5 proteins bound to the E-boxes of the Dbp gene (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Recombinant TIP60GST acetylated recombinant BMAL1GST at Lys538.
source: Recombinant TIP60GST acetylated recombinant BMAL1GST at Lys538 (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by in vitro acetylation assay data shown in Figure 5B

claim: In TIP60-deficient MEFs, Lys538 acetylation of endogenous BMAL1 was markedly reduced.
source: and, in TIP60-deficient MEFs, Lys538 acetylation of endogenous BMAL1 was markedly reduced (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C

claim: When endogenous TIP60 was replaced by TIP60C369A;E403Q in the Bmal1-LUC reporter cell line, luciferase rhythms and mRNA rhythms of endogenous Dbp were abolished.
source: When endogenous TIP60 was replaced by TIP60C369A;E403Q in the Bmal1-LUC reporter cell line, luciferase rhythms and mRNA rhythms of endogenous Dbp were abolished (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence and mRNA expression data shown in Figure 5D and E

claim: BMAL1 is a substrate of TIP60.
source: Collectively, these data provide strong evidence that BMAL1 is a substrate of TIP60.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing TIP60 acetylates BMAL1

claim: In confluent TIP60-deficient Dex synchronized fibroblasts, BMAL1 was hypoacetylated.
source: Indeed, in confluent TIP60-deficient Dex synchronized fibroblasts, BMAL1 was hypoacetylated (Figures 5C and 6A)
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figures 5C and 6A

claim: In TIP60-deficient fibroblasts, there was a major loss of interaction between BMAL1 and BRD4.
source: and there was a major loss of interaction between BMAL1 and BRD4 (Figure 6A and B)
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A and B

claim: In TIP60-deficient fibroblasts, there was a major loss of interaction between BMAL1 and CDK9.
source: as well as between BMAL1 and CDK9 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6C

claim: In TIP60-deficient fibroblasts, enrichment of BRD4 and CDK9 at the TSS of Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1 genes was strongly reduced.
source: ChIP experiments showed that enrichment of BRD4 and CDK9 at the TSS of Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1 genes was strongly reduced and Ser2-phosphorylated Pol II occupancy was diminished (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: In TIP60-deficient fibroblasts, Ser2-phosphorylated Pol II occupancy was diminished at Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1 genes.
source: ChIP experiments showed that enrichment of BRD4 and CDK9 at the TSS of Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1 genes was strongly reduced and Ser2-phosphorylated Pol II occupancy was diminished (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: Deletion of Tip60 did not affect TFIIEα recruitment to the TSS of Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1 genes.
source: Since TIP60 acetylates BMAL1, TIP60 deletion should not affect transcription initiation, which was indeed the case. Deletion of Tip60 did not affect TFIIEα recruitment to the TSS of Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1 genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: TIP60-mediated acetylation of BMAL1 is an essential element of the positive limb of the circadian clock oscillator.
source: Collectively, our experiments provide evidence that TIP60-mediated acetylation of BMAL1 is an essential element of the positive limb of the circadian clock oscillator.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results

claim: TIP60-mediated BMAL1 acetylation leads to the recruitment of BRD4 and of the pause release factor P-TEFb to clock gene TSSs.
source: TIP60-mediated BMAL1 acetylation leads to the recruitment of BRD4 and of the pause release factor P-TEFb to clock gene TSSs.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results

claim: Recruitment of BRD4 and P-TEFb allows productive elongation of CLOCK-BMAL1-controlled genes.
source: This, in turn, allows productive elongation of CLOCK-BMAL1-controlled genes.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results

claim: Approximately 24 hr after synchronization of the cells, the strongest enrichment of BMAL1 and of acetylated BMAL1 at the promoters of Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1 genes was observed.
source: Approximately 24 hr after synchronization of the cells, we observed the strongest enrichment of BMAL1 and of acetylated BMAL1 at the promoters of Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1 genes (Figure 7A, green).
evidence: Supported by time-course ChIP data shown in Figure 7A

claim: The concentration of acetylated BMAL1 in nuclear extracts showed its maximum at approximately 24 hr after synchronization.
source: The concentration of acetylated BMAL1 in nuclear extracts also showed its maximum by that time (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7B

claim: The occupancy of BRD4 peaked at target gene promoters at approximately 24 hr after synchronization.
source: In parallel, the occupancy of BRD4 peaked at target gene promoters (Figure 7A)
evidence: Supported by time-course ChIP data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Ser2 phosphorylation of Pol II showed a maximum at approximately 24 hr after synchronization.
source: and Ser2 phosphorylation of Pol II showed a maximum (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by time-course ChIP data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: The abundance of Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1 mRNA peaked between 24 and 28 hr after synchronization.
source: Consequently, the abundance of Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1 mRNA peaked between 24 and 28 hr (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by mRNA expression data shown in Figure 7A

claim: TIP60-dependent BRD4 recruitment, Pol II pause release, and productive elongation are precisely timed over the circadian cycle.
source: Taken together, our data show that TIP60-dependent BRD4 recruitment, Pol II pause release, and productive elongation are precisely timed over the circadian cycle and in this way exert a temporal control over the circadian clock oscillator.
evidence: Inferred from the time-course experiments showing coordinated timing of these events

claim: At the onset of the circadian cycle, the circadian repressor protein CRY1 is associated with chromatin-bound CLOCK-BMAL1 located near Pol II.
source: Genome-wide ChIP studies (Koike et al., 2012; Menet et al., 2012; Rey et al., 2011) show that at the onset of the circadian cycle, the circadian repressor protein CRY1 is associated with chromatin-bound CLOCK-BMAL1 located near Pol II.
evidence: Supported by citations to Koike et al., 2012; Menet et al., 2012; Rey et al., 2011

claim: In the CRY1-CLOCK-BMAL1 complex, Pol II is bound to the clock gene promoters but is not competent to drive RNA synthesis.
source: In this complex Pol II is bound to the clock gene promoters but is not competent to drive RNA synthesis.
evidence: Inferred from the genome-wide ChIP studies

claim: At the onset of the circadian cycle, Pol II is phosphorylated at Ser5, which is indicative for promoter-proximal pausing and recruitment of the mRNA capping complex to Pol II.
source: At this time in the circadian cycle Pol II is phosphorylated at Ser5 (Koike et al., 2012), which is indicative for promoter-proximal pausing and recruitment of the mRNA capping complex to Pol II (Harlen and Churchman, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Koike et al., 2012 and Harlen and Churchman, 2017

claim: Strong enrichment of Pol II at the TSS of the Nr1d1 gene was observed at the onset of the circadian cycle, suggesting that Pol II is in a paused state.
source: Evidence for Pol II pausing to occur at this time at circadian promoters can also be found in global run-on experiments measuring transcriptionally engaged Pol II during the circadian cycle (Fang et al., 2014). Strong enrichment of Pol II at the TSS of the Nr1d1 gene was observed at the onset of the circadian cycle, suggesting that Pol II is in a paused state.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fang et al., 2014

claim: Genome-wide and circadian time-resolved quantitative analysis of Pol II abundance shows a peak of Pol II binding at TSSs, but not the gene bodies of clock genes, at the onset of the circadian cycle.
source: Genome-wide and circadian time-resolved quantitative analysis of Pol II abundance at TSSs and gene bodies show a peak of Pol II binding at TSSs, but not the gene bodies of clock genes, at the onset of the circadian cycle (Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2018

claim: A circadian control of promoter proximal pausing and Pol II pause release would provide mechanisms capable to accurately time circadian transcription.
source: A circadian control of promoter proximal pausing and also of Pol II pause release would provide mechanisms capable to accurately time circadian transcription (Jonkers and Lis, 2015; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jonkers and Lis, 2015; Liu et al., 2015

claim: Pause release involves a TIP60-mediated on-chromatin acetylation of Lys538 of BMAL1.
source: In the present work, we have addressed the mechanism of the circadian regulation of Pol II pause release with a focus on proteins that are known to mediate this process. We propose that pause release involves a TIP60-mediated on-chromatin acetylation of Lys538 of BMAL1.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings

claim: BMAL1 acetylation allows the recruitment of the co-activator BRD4 to AcBMAL1.
source: BMAL1 acetylation allows the recruitment of the co-activator BRD4 to AcBMAL1.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings

claim: BRD4 recruits the pause release factor P-TEFb, whose kinase subunit CDK9 then phosphorylates Ser2 of Pol II leading to a release of Pol II from the paused state enabling productive elongation of E-box-containing circadian genes.
source: BRD4, in turn, recruits the pause release factor P-TEFb, whose kinase subunit CDK9 then phosphorylates Ser2 of Pol II leading to a release of Pol II from the paused state enabling productive elongation of E-box-containing circadian genes (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings

claim: In TIP60-deficient cells, Lys538 acetylation of BMAL1 was strongly diminished, BRD4-P-TEFb recruitment was reduced, and the expression of Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1 genes was dampened.
source: In TIP60-deficient cells, Lys538 acetylation of BMAL1 was strongly diminished, BRD4-P-TEFb recruitment was reduced, and the expression of Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1 genes was dampened.
evidence: Summarizes experimental findings from multiple figures

claim: BMAL1K538R mutant protein still interacted with TIP60, but recruitment of BRD4 and P-TEFb to the complex was reduced and Pol II pause release and productive elongation were diminished.
source: If acetylation of BMAL at Lys538 was prevented by a Lys to Arg substitution (BMAL1K538R), this mutant protein still interacted with TIP60, but recruitment of BRD4 and P-TEFb to the complex was reduced and Pol II pause release and productive elongation were diminished.
evidence: Summarizes experimental findings from Figure 2 and Figure 5

claim: The dysregulation of the circadian rhythm of locomotor activity in the mouse and perturbation of circadian gene expression in the SCN and in MEFs provide strong genetic evidence for a key role of TIP60 in the circadian clock.
source: The dysregulation of the circadian rhythm of locomotor activity in the mouse and perturbation of circadian gene expression in the SCN and in MEFs provide strong genetic evidence for a key role of TIP60 in the circadian clock.
evidence: Inferred from the combined in vivo and in vitro experimental results

claim: Rhythmic control of Pol II pause release may be a main process in which TIP60 is involved.
source: Our studies of TIP60-deficient MEFs suggest that rhythmic control of Pol II pause release may be a main process in which TIP60 is involved.
evidence: Inferred from the TIP60-deficient MEF experiments

claim: Pol II pause release is an additional regulatory step that contributes to the temporal control of the mammalian circadian clock.
source: Our studies thus implicate Pol II pause release as an additional regulatory step that contributes to the temporal control of the mammalian circadian clock.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results

claim: TIP60 is evolutionarily highly conserved and is involved in the regulation of a series of cellular processes.
source: TIP60 is evolutionarily highly conserved and is involved in the regulation of a series of cellular processes (see Introduction).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge referenced in the Introduction

claim: TIP60 has the role of an enzymatically active cofactor in larger multiprotein complexes.
source: Thereby, TIP60 has the role of an enzymatically active cofactor in larger multiprotein complexes (Jacquet et al., 2016; Judes et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jacquet et al., 2016; Judes et al., 2015

claim: The three genes studied (Dbp, Per1, Nr1d1) are robustly rhythmic and clock phase-specific genes that harbor multiple CLOCK-BMAL1 binding sites such as the tandem E-box motif.
source: Our studies are based on three robustly rhythmic and clock phase-specific genes that harbor multiple CLOCK-BMAL1 binding sites such as the tandem E-box motif (E1-E2) (Paquet et al., 2008; Rey et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Paquet et al., 2008; Rey et al., 2011

claim: There are many other strongly rhythmic, phase specific CLOCK-BMAL1-target genes that also harbor multiple E-boxes.
source: There are many other strongly rhythmic, phase specific CLOCK-BMAL1-target genes that also harbor multiple E-boxes (Rey et al., 2011; Shimomura et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rey et al., 2011; Shimomura et al., 2013

claim: Regulation by Pol II pause release could extend to the entire class of E-box controlled clock genes.
source: This suggests that regulation by Pol II pause release could extend to the entire class of E-box controlled clock genes.
evidence: Speculated based on the findings for the three genes studied

claim: In fibroblasts and in the SCN, deletion of TIP60 resulted in a nearly complete loss of rhythmic expression of numerous circadian genes suggesting that in these tissues and for these genes TIP60 function is non-redundant with CBP/p300 acetyltransferase.
source: We found that in fibroblasts, but also in the SCN, deletion of TIP60 resulted in a nearly complete loss of rhythmic expression of numerous circadian genes suggesting that in these tissues and for these genes TIP60 function is non-redundant with CBP/p300 acetyltransferase that also binds to circadian promoters.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing loss of rhythmicity upon TIP60 deletion

claim: Recombinant TIP60 directly acetylates recombinant BMAL1.
source: The strongest argument for BMAL1 being a substrate of TIP60 is that recombinant TIP60 directly acetylates recombinant BMAL1.
evidence: Supported by in vitro acetylation assay data shown in Figure 5B

claim: p300 can acetylate BMAL1 at lysine 500.
source: Although p300 can acetylate BMAL1 it does so at lysine 500 (Weinert et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weinert et al., 2018

claim: The abundance of BRD4 at clock gene promoters was drastically reduced in BMAL1K538R cells.
source: The abundance of BRD4 at clock gene promoters was drastically reduced in BMAL1K538R cells, but it is likely that there are other acetylated substrates, such as histones H3 and H4 (Etchegaray et al., 2003; Koike et al., 2012; Ripperger and Schibler, 2006; Vollmers et al., 2012), to which BRD4 could also be recruited and affect the circadian clock.
evidence: Supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2B

claim: There are other acetylated substrates, such as histones H3 and H4, to which BRD4 could also be recruited and affect the circadian clock.
source: The abundance of BRD4 at clock gene promoters was drastically reduced in BMAL1K538R cells, but it is likely that there are other acetylated substrates, such as histones H3 and H4 (Etchegaray et al., 2003; Koike et al., 2012; Ripperger and Schibler, 2006; Vollmers et al., 2012), to which BRD4 could also be recruited and affect the circadian clock.
evidence: Supported by citations to Etchegaray et al., 2003; Koike et al., 2012; Ripperger and Schibler, 2006; Vollmers et al., 2012

claim: It is proposed that CLOCK acetylates its heterodimeric partner BMAL1 at lysine 538, which leads to recruitment of CRY protein and initiates the repression phase of the circadian cycle.
source: It is proposed that CLOCK acetylates its heterodimeric partner BMAL1 at lysine 538. This leads to recruitment of CRY protein and, thus, initiates the repression phase of the circadian cycle (Hirayama et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hirayama et al., 2007

claim: TIP60-mediated acetylation of BMAL1 occurs during the activation phase of the cycle.
source: We found that TIP60-mediated acetylation of BMAL1 occurs during the activation phase of the cycle, which is consistent with the data of Nakahata and co-workers (Nakahata et al., 2008; Nakahata et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by time-course data shown in Figure 7 and citations to Nakahata et al., 2008; Nakahata et al., 2009

claim: The finding of strong acetylation of Lys538 of BMAL1 in CLOCK-deficient fibroblasts raises doubt about the efficiency of CLOCK as an acetyltransferase for BMAL1.
source: Our finding of strong acetylation of Lys538 of BMAL1 in CLOCK-deficient fibroblasts and the absence of an effect on the BMAL1 acetylation status in a reaction with a catalytically inactive CLOCK mutant protein raises some doubt about the efficiency of CLOCK as an acetyltransferase for BMAL1.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3B

claim: CLOCK acetylates argininosuccinate synthase in the cytosol of U2OS cells.
source: It is noteworthy that CLOCK acetylates argininosuccinate synthase in the cytosol of U2OS cells (Lin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin et al., 2017

claim: One possibility for BMAL1 deacetylation during the repression phase is a SIRT1-dependent deacetylation of BMAL1.
source: TIP60 acetylates BMAL1 during the activation phase, but it is not clear by which mechanism BMAL1 is deacetylated during the repression phase. One possibility is a SIRT1-dependent deacetylation of BMAL1 (Nakahata et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakahata et al., 2008

claim: Recruitment of histone deacetylases by PER to the CLOCK-BMAL1 heterodimer would lead to deacetylation of BMAL1.
source: Alternatively, recruitment of histone deacetylases by PER to the CLOCK-BMAL1 heterodimer (Duong et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2014) would lead to deacetylation of BMAL1.
evidence: Supported by citations to Duong et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2014

claim: Promoter-associated acetylated BMAL1 could be subject to rapid proteolytic turnover obviating the need for a specific deacetylase.
source: Another possibility is that promoter-associated acetylated BMAL1 could be subject to rapid proteolytic turnover (Stratmann et al., 2012) obviating the need for a specific deacetylase.
evidence: Supported by citation to Stratmann et al., 2012

claim: The positive limb of the circadian clock requires TIP60-mediated acetylation of BMAL1, at least for the genes studied.
source: Taken together, our study provides evidence that the positive limb of the circadian clock requires TIP60-mediated acetylation of BMAL1, at least for the genes studied here.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results

claim: TIP60-mediated acetylation of BMAL1 could allow a precise and synchronous expression of E-box-containing clock genes and contribute to robustness and precision of the circadian clock.
source: This could allow a precise and synchronous expression of E-box-containing clock genes and in this way also contribute to robustness and precision of the circadian clock.
evidence: Speculated based on the experimental findings

claim: Robust and synchronous expression are the hallmarks of genes involved in stimulus-controlled pathways, whose transcription is also often regulated through Pol II pause release.
source: Robust and synchronous expression are the hallmarks of genes involved in stimulus-controlled pathways, whose transcription is also often regulated through Pol II pause release (Jonkers and Lis, 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Sawarkar et al., 2012; Siegal and Rushlow, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jonkers and Lis, 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Sawarkar et al., 2012; Siegal and Rushlow, 2012

claim: In BMAL1K538R expressing cells, the interaction between BMAL1 and BRD4/CDK9 was markedly reduced.
source: Immunoprecipitation experiments showed that in BMAL1K538R expressing cells this interaction was markedly reduced (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A

claim: BMAL1K538R mutant cells showed a diminished recruitment of BRD4 and of the P-TEFb subunit CDK9 to the TSS of Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1.
source: ChIP experiments demonstrated that BMAL1K538R mutant cells showed a diminished recruitment of BRD4 and of the P-TEFb subunit CDK9 to the TSS of Dbp (Figure 2B), Per1, and Nr1d1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: In BMAL1K538R mutant cells, enrichment of Ser2-phosphorylated Pol II was markedly reduced.
source: In addition, enrichment of Ser2-phosphorylated Pol II was markedly reduced (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: In BMAL1K538R cells, virtually no rhythmic luciferase reporter expression was recorded for any of the three clones.
source: In BMAL1K538R cells virtually no rhythmic luciferase reporter expression was recorded for any of the three clones (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 2C

claim: In BMAL1K538R cells, there was a pronounced reduction of peak expression of endogenous Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1 mRNAs.
source: In addition, in these cells there was a pronounced reduction of peak expression of endogenous Dbp (Figure 2D), Per1, and Nr1d1 mRNAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by mRNA expression data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F

claim: The occupancy of the general transcription factor TFIIEα at the TSS of Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1 genes was not affected in BMAL1K538R mutant cells.
source: However, the occupancy of the general transcription factor TFIIEα (part of the Pol II transcription initiation complex; Sainsbury et al., 2015) at the TSS of Dbp, Per1, and Nr1d1 genes was not affected in mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G

claim: Transcription elongation, and not initiation, is the process that is primarily regulated by acetylation of BMAL1.
source: This favors the idea that transcription elongation, and not initiation, is the process that is primarily regulated by acetylation of BMAL1.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect on TFIIEα recruitment in BMAL1K538R cells

claim: Acetylated BMAL1 recruits BRD4-P-TEFb to E-box-containing circadian clock genes which results in a release of Pol II from its paused state, thereby allowing productive elongation.
source: Our data support a mechanism in which acetylated BMAL1 recruits BRD4-P and TEFb to E-box-containing circadian clock genes which then results in a release of Pol II from its paused state, thereby allowing productive elongation.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on the combined experimental findings
